title: Beginner To Master | Viewer Games | Chess Speedrun

moves.spoken: We answer the king-pawn with the Sicilian and head for the Najdorf, my main opening from 1600 all the way to 2500.
For the 1400-1500 crowd I'd recommend the Accelerated Dragon, but here we go for the Najdorf itself, starting with the little d6.
He opens with d4, the Open Sicilian, and after the trades we reach the tabiya.

Now the move that defines it: a6, the Najdorf. Its simple purpose is to take the b5-square away — no bishop or knight check on b5 — and to prepare a later b7-b5, grabbing queenside space, an idea that runs through almost every Sicilian.
He chooses f3, the English Attack — the signal that he's going to castle long and storm my king with his pawns.
teaches: English Attack: f3 prepares queenside castling and a kingside pawn storm

moves.spoken: And here's the move I grew up on: e5, kicking the knight. The downside is obvious — it weakens the d6-pawn and gouges a permanent hole on d5. The pawn and the square in front of it go weak together, as they so often do.
teaches: A pawn push weakens the square in front of it
...e5 in the Najdorf concedes d5 for dynamic play

moves.spoken: He retreats the knight to b3. What Black gets for that weak pawn and weak square is dynamic, concrete counterplay — that's exactly why the Sicilian is so sharp and theoretical.
First we solve our light-squared bishop, developing it to e6 to lend cover to d5, so he can't just plant a knight there and blockade.
teaches: Cover the weak square before the opponent occupies it

moves.spoken: He pins with the bishop to g5 — not actually the main move; Be3 is. And that misplaced bishop is going to cost him dearly, because it sits right where his own g-pawn wants to go.
We simply unpin by developing the bishop to e7. Note we avoid h6: that pawn would become a hook his g-pawn could latch onto once we castle short, so we keep our kingside pawns intact.
teaches: Don\u2019t create a pawn hook in front of your king

moves.spoken: The queen-knight reroutes to d7, where the two knights defend one another — the classic Najdorf configuration.
teaches: The b8-knight belongs on d7 in this structure

moves.spoken: He castles queenside; we castle short. Opposite wings — now the race is on, each side storming the other's king.
teaches: Opposite-side castling means a pawn-storm race

moves.spoken: He starts the storm with h4, intending g4-g5 to pry my king open. We answer on the other flank.
This is where a6 pays off: we counterattack with b5, and both sides are charging on opposite sides of the board. My follow-up is b4, a5, a4.
teaches: Race the opponent\u2019s attack with your own — tempo is everything

moves.spoken: We push b4, hitting his knight — and watch how much time that stranded g5-bishop costs him: it blocks his g-pawn, so the storm he wanted in one move now takes several.
teaches: A misplaced bishop that blocks your own pawn storm loses crucial tempi

moves.spoken: He drops the knight into d5. We don't let it marinate on such a fine square.
And we take with the bishop, not the knight — because recapturing with the knight lets him take back and trap our e6-bishop, while his g5-bishop stays defended by the h-pawn.
teaches: Choose the recapture that doesn\u2019t leave a piece trapped

moves.spoken: After he recaptures, that d5-pawn is like a dental filling: it closes the center and walls off our weak d6-pawn from the d-file, sealing the very weakness he was pressuring.
teaches: A closed center can neutralize your own structural weakness

moves.spoken: With the center shut, we roll on with a5 and a4 — pure, sharp Najdorf, which fits my style like a glove.
He tucks the king toward safety, but we're a step ahead in the race. Now we bring in the beef — pawns alone won't break through; the pieces have to join.
teaches: A pawn storm needs pieces behind it to break through

moves.spoken: The queen swings to b6, sidestepping while it connects the rooks and clears the way for a rook to c8.
Now b3 — we sacrifice a pawn to blast open the files around his king.
teaches: Sacrifice pawns to open lines toward the enemy king

moves.spoken: We crash through on b3, opening the b-file, and prepare a frontal assault against the exposed king.
The exchange sacrifice on a2 — cutting the legs out from under his knight and ripping the a-file wide open.

Ra8+ chases the king, then we scoop the knight back with the queen. And the key lesson: sacrifices live on a sliding scale — an exchange sac is nothing like a queen sac. Even if the attack fizzles we're only down the exchange, so there's no reason to be scared.
teaches: Sacrifices exist on a sliding scale — risk the exchange freely

moves.spoken: Look how many attackers we have. Even the d7-knight, seemingly outside the zone, comes roaring in with Nc5. The Najdorf poses very human problems that are hard to defend at the board.
plans: Bring the d7-knight in via c5
Pile every piece onto the open king

moves.spoken: He plays Qc3 to trade queens, but that lifts the defender off his d1-rook.
teaches: Beware trades that undefend a piece

moves.spoken: We collect on d5 — up a piece, his position collapsing. The game is over.
With a knight loitering next to his open king, we finish with the fork. Clean game.
teaches: A knight near an exposed king is a forking weapon
